summary: This informational memo provides design and implementation details of a multicast server (MCS) building on RFC 2022 and describes using several MCSs per group for fault tolerance. It works with existing MARS servers and clients unchanged.

plainLanguage.summary: One postman copies a letter for everyone in a group, and a backup postman stands ready if he is sick.

subtitle: Using a relay server to distribute multicast messages over ATM networks.

tldr.problem: ATM networks need to deliver messages from one sender to multiple receivers (multicast), but ATM uses connection-oriented virtual circuits that are expensive to set up directly between senders and all receivers.
tldr.mechanism: A Multicast Server (MCS) acts as a proxy: sources send their data to the MCS, which forwards it to all group members on a single point-to-multipoint virtual circuit, and multiple MCSs can stand by to take over if the active one fails.
tldr.outcome: This reduces the number of virtual circuits needed and provides fault tolerance without requiring changes to the MARS server that manages group membership.

facts.label: Election confirmation threshold
facts.value: At least half of the inactive MCSs must respond

today: RFC 2149 is Informational and describes a technique for reliable multicast in ATM networks. It builds on RFC 2022, which defined MARS itself. This RFC is not currently widely deployed as ATM has largely been superseded by IP-based networking, but the multicast server architecture principle remains relevant in other contexts.

sections.title: Multicast in ATM Networks
sections.content:
ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode) networks use virtual circuits (VCs) to route data between endpoints. Unlike IP, which broadcasts to multiple receivers, ATM requires explicit connection setup. The MARS (Multicast Address Resolution Server) maps layer 3 group addresses (like IP multicast addresses) to lists of ATM addresses of group members.

When a sender wants to multicast in an ATM cluster, it has two choices: set up a point-to-multipoint VC directly to each group member (the VC Mesh approach), or use an intermediary Multicast Server (MCS) as a proxy. The MCS approach trades some setup time for simpler resource management.
sections.plainLanguage: ATM networks set up dedicated phone lines between parties. Instead of the sender calling everyone in the group, the sender calls one operator, who then forwards the call to everyone.

sections.title: How a Multicast Server Works
sections.content:
An MCS is a dedicated server in the ATM cluster. Sources transmitting to an MCS-based group send unicast (point-to-point) data to the MCS. The MCS maintains a single point-to-multipoint VC to all group members and forwards every packet it receives from sources onto this shared tree.

The MCS registers with the MARS to announce it will serve a particular layer 3 group or groups. When group members join (via MARS), the MCS learns this through the ServerControlVC, a point-to-multipoint tree from MARS to all MCSs. The MCS then adds the new member to its outgoing VC by sending LMULTI-ADD signals to the ATM signaling layer.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail center registers with the post office to handle letters for "Book Club Tuesday." When someone joins the club, the post office tells the mail center, and the mail center adds them to the delivery list.

sections.title: Control Procedures and Membership Updates
sections.content:
The MCS exchanges several control messages with MARS. MARS-MSERV registers the MCS as a server; MARS-REQUEST and MARS-MULTI retrieve the current group membership; and the MCS monitors MARS-SJOIN and MARS-SLEAVE announcements on the ServerControlVC to track members joining and leaving.

If an MCS receives a layer 3 packet but has no outgoing VC yet (because no members exist), it triggers a new MARS-REQUEST to refresh membership and only then sets up the VC. The point-to-multipoint VC from the MCS remains open even when idle, to avoid the delay of re-establishing it when new traffic arrives.
sections.plainLanguage: The mail center asks the post office, "Who is in Book Club Tuesday?" The post office answers with the list. When someone joins or leaves, the post office announces it on a shared bulletin board all mail centers read.

sections.title: Fault Tolerance with Multiple MCSs
sections.content:
Since a single MCS is a single point of failure, the RFC supports multiple MCSs per group. A predetermined list of MCSs (the mcslist) is configured at startup. The first MCS in the list becomes the active MCS and registers with MARS; the others become inactive standby servers.

The active MCS sends periodic HELLO heartbeat messages to the inactive MCSs on a point-to-multipoint VC. These messages carry a HelloInterval (the time between heartbeats) and a DeadFactor (a multiplier). If an inactive MCS does not receive a HELLO within HelloInterval × DeadFactor seconds, it assumes the active MCS has failed and initiates an election. The candidate MCS sends HELLO messages with State=No-Op; if it hears from at least half of the other inactive MCSs, it becomes the new active MCS and registers with MARS.
sections.plainLanguage: The main mail center sends a "I am alive" message every 10 seconds to the backup centers. If a backup doesn't hear for 30 seconds, it assumes the main center failed and takes over, announcing itself to the post office.

sections.title: HELLO Message Structure
sections.content:
HELLO messages are used for heartbeats and election. Each message contains sender and receiver ATM address lengths, a state field (No-Op or Elected), a type code (5), HelloInterval and DeadFactor values, the IP multicast group address being served, and variable-length sender and receiver ATM addresses.

The active MCS sets State to Elected and Receiver Length to zero (because it is multicast to all inactive MCSs). During election, candidates set State to No-Op and send to specific inactive MCSs. Once a candidate receives confirmation from at least half of the inactive servers, it becomes the new active MCS and begins sending HELLO messages with State=Elected.
sections.plainLanguage: The heartbeat message is like a postcard: "I am center number 1, and I'm awake. Check in with me every 10 seconds." If the backup gets one, it resets its timer. If the timer runs out, the backup sends postcards asking, "Can you hear me?" If enough backups answer, one of them becomes the new center.
